recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say which nearby value you start from, and the formula you then apply.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Choose the nearby exact point
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the whole choice of method sits here: name x = 81, Δx = 1 and f′(81) = 1/18. An examiner reads this line to see whether the nearest perfect square was found.
lines: Let f(x) = √x. Then f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f′(x)·Δx
81 is the nearest perfect square to 82, and √81 = 9 exactly

recall.must_convey: That x = 81 is chosen because √81 = 9 is exact, Δx = 1, and f′(81) = 1/18.

the nearest perfect square is eighty one so delta x is one

daggara unna perfect square eighty one teesukovali, delta x one
start from nine and correct it

steps.why: The method only works from a point where the function is already known exactly. 81 is the nearest perfect square to 82, so the estimate starts at 9 with no calculator, and Δx = 1 is small next to 81.
common_mistakes: Choosing x = 82 itself, which leaves the square root still unknown.
Writing f′(x) = 1/√x and losing the 2 in the denominator.
steps.memory_tip: For a square root, find the nearest perfect square; for a cube root, the nearest perfect cube. Δx carries whatever is left over.

steps.label: Apply the approximation formula
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 1/18 = 0.0555… recurs, so keep four decimal places before rounding. 82 is above 81, so the correction is added.

accept: nine plus zero point zero five five five
the answer is nine point zero five five six

steps.why: f′(x)·Δx is the correction the tangent line at x = 81 predicts. The true value is 9.055385, so this estimate is high by about 0.00017 — the straight line sits slightly above the curve, which is why every square-root estimate of this kind comes out a little large.
common_mistakes: Rounding 9 + 0.0556 to 9.06 and losing the decimal places the question is asking for.
steps.memory_tip: New value ≈ old value + slope × step. The step keeps its sign, so an upward move adds.
